questions.question: Explain why atoms bond, and describe the covalent bonding in water and in nitrogen gas, naming the bond types and lone pairs involved.
questions.expected_answer: Atoms bond to reach a full outer energy level — the stable, low-energy electron arrangement of a noble gas: eight outer electrons for most atoms, two for hydrogen. Covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms, each atom counting the shared pair toward its own outer level. In water, H two O, oxygen has six valence electrons with two unpaired; it shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms — two single bonds — and keeps two lone pairs. Each hydrogen then has two electrons and the oxygen eight. In nitrogen gas, N two, each nitrogen has five valence electrons and needs three more, so the two atoms share three pairs — a triple bond — with one lone pair remaining on each atom. The triple bond is extremely strong, which is why nitrogen gas is so unreactive.

questions.question: Describe how the ionic bond in calcium chloride forms, derive its formula from periodic-table positions, and explain why ionic compounds are brittle, have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved.
questions.expected_answer: Calcium, a group 2 metal, transfers its two valence electrons — one to each of two chlorine atoms, group 17 non-metals. Calcium becomes the cation Ca two plus and each chlorine becomes the anion Cl minus; the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions. Balancing charge to zero, one plus-two calcium needs two minus-one chlorides, so the formula unit is CaCl two. The ions stack into a giant crystal lattice with attractions in all directions, not into molecules. High melting point: melting must overcome strong attractions running throughout the lattice. Brittleness: shifting a layer brings like charges face to face, so attraction becomes repulsion and the crystal cleaves. Conduction: in the solid the ions are locked in the lattice, but when molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry charge.

questions.question: Describe metallic bonding and use it to explain conduction and malleability. Then calculate the relative molecular mass of ammonia (N = 14; H = 1) and the relative formula mass of magnesium bromide (Mg = 24; Br = 80).
questions.expected_answer: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised valence electrons they release, which belong to the metal as a whole. Conduction: the delocalised electrons are already free to move, so they flow when a potential difference is applied, and they also transfer heat efficiently. Malleability: when layers of ions are pushed past one another, the electron sea flows around the new arrangement so the bonding survives — the metal bends instead of shattering. Ammonia, NH three: 14 plus three times 1 = 17. Magnesium bromide, MgBr two: 24 plus two times 80 = 24 plus 160 = 184. The method is the same for both — inventory the atoms, multiply each count by its relative atomic mass, add — but the result is called relative molecular mass for the covalent molecule and relative formula mass for the ionic compound.
